Compare the spatial expression patterns of genes between two samples

Source: R/compareSpatial.R
compareSpatial.Rd

For every gene measured in two samples on one shared grid of pixels, compareSpatial() tests whether the gene's expression patterns are correlated beyond what the spatial autocorrelation of each pattern alone would produce (spatial correlation test), and how often the two samples' values at the same pixel are within a fold change of each other (spatial similarity). It returns one row per gene.

Usage

compareSpatial(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  assay = 1,
  genes = NULL,
  tests = c("correlation", "similarity"),
  nPermutations = 10000,
  exceedances = 10,
  delta = c(0.01, 0.05, seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1)),
  maxDistPrctile = 0.25,
  minDetected = NULL,
  surrogate = c("remap", "gaussian"),
  foldChange = 1,
  minQuantile = 0.05,
  minPixels = 0.1,
  adjustMethod = "BH",
  seed = 0L,
  nThreads = getOption("STcompare.nThreads", 1L),
  progress = interactive(),
  verbose = TRUE,
  keepNulls = FALSE
)

Arguments

x, y

Two SpatialExperiment objects with the same pixels, for example the elements of the list returned by one SEraster::rasterizeGeneExpression() call. Alternatively x is a list of two such objects and y is NULL, such as the list returned by SEraster::rasterizeGeneExpression(list(a = ..., b = ...)); the names of the list, if any, are used as the sample labels (otherwise "x" and "y").

assay

The assay to use: a name or an index, used for both objects, or two names or two indices, one per object. Default: the first assay.

genes

The genes (row names) to compare. Default NULL: every gene present in both objects (a message says how many were dropped). Genes given here must be present in both objects.

tests

Which tests to run: "correlation" (the spatial correlation test with permutations) and/or "similarity" (no permutations).

nPermutations

The largest number of permutations per gene; the smallest possible p-value is 1 / (nPermutations + 1). Default 10000.

exceedances

The number of null correlations at least as extreme as the observed one after which a gene stops early (\(h\) of Besag and Clifford). The relative standard error of a p-value is about 1 / sqrt(exceedances). Default 10; Inf gives every gene exactly nPermutations permutations.

delta

The candidate smoothing bandwidths, as shares of the pixels in the kernel's window (values in (0, 1]). Values that leave fewer than 2 pixels in the window (\(\lfloor N\delta \rfloor < 2\) for \(N\) shared pixels) are dropped with a message. The default adds 0.01 and 0.05 to seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1), the grid the authors used for the kidney and MERFISH analyses: with the shorter grid, delta star is often its smallest value.

maxDistPrctile

The quantile of the pairwise pixel distances up to which the variograms are computed. Default 0.25.

minDetected

The smallest share of the shared pixels at which a gene must be detected, in each sample, to be tested for correlation (see Rarely detected genes in Details); 0 tests every gene that is not constant. Default NULL, which depends on surrogate: 0 (no filter) with "remap", whose p-values are calibrated for rarely detected genes, and \(\sqrt{N}\) of the \(N\) shared pixels (18 of 311, 47 of 2170) with "gaussian", whose p-values are far too small for such genes. The number of pixels asked for is recorded in attr(result, "params")$minDetectedPixels.

surrogate

How the surrogates of the correlation test take their values (see Rank-remapped surrogates in Details): "remap" (the default) gives each surrogate the gene's own values, in the surrogate's rank order, so that it has exactly the gene's distribution of values, which calibrates the p-values of sparse and skewed genes; "gaussian" uses them as the smoothing and the added noise leave them, the surrogates of the legacy functions and of the published analyses.

foldChange

The similarity band: pixels with \(|\log_2(y / x)| \le\) foldChange are similar. Default 1 (within two-fold).

minQuantile

The quantile of each gene's values in each sample used as its expression threshold for the similarity. Default 0.05.

minPixels

The smallest share of the pixels that must pass the threshold for the similarity to be computed. Default 0.1.

adjustMethod

The multiple-testing adjustment of pValuePermute across the tested genes, which gives pValuePermuteAdj; one of stats::p.adjust.methods. Default "BH".

seed

An integer seed for the permutations and the noise. Default 0.

nThreads

The number of threads. Default getOption("STcompare.nThreads", 1L), so it can be set once per session with options(STcompare.nThreads = 8). The results do not depend on it.

progress

Show a progress line (with an estimate of the remaining time) while the permutations run. Default interactive(). It is written as a message, so suppressMessages() also hides it.

verbose

Show informative messages: genes or deltas that were dropped, genes whose delta star is at the edge of the grid, p-values limited by nPermutations, and the total time. Default TRUE.

keepNulls

Keep the null correlations and delta stars of every permutation in attr(result, "details"). Default FALSE.

Value

A data frame of class "STcompareResult" with one row per gene (row names are the genes) and the columns below, in this order. The columns of a test that was not run are absent. The column names are those of the legacy functions, spatialCorrelationGeneExp() and spatialSimilarity(), where the two report the same quantity; the differences in meaning are stated for each column. In the formulas, \(L\) is the number of permutations of the gene (the nPermutations column), and \(b_x\) and \(b_y\) count its null correlations whose absolute value is at least the observed \(|r|\) when x and when y is permuted.

gene

The gene (also the row name).

nPixels

The number of shared pixels, the same for every gene.

correlationCoef

Pearson's correlation \(r\) of the gene's values in x and y over the shared pixels (cor()). Reported for every gene with finite values, tested or not. The same as in spatialCorrelationGeneExp().

pValueNaive

The analytical p-value of cor.test(), which assumes that the pixels are independent. For reference only: under spatial autocorrelation it is far too small. The same as in spatialCorrelationGeneExp().

pValuePermuteX

The sequential permutation p-value of the direction that permutes x, \((b_x + 1) / (L + 1)\), at the common stopping point \(L\) of the two directions. Not adjusted. Descriptive: when a gene stops early, the direction that did not reach exceedances has an inflated value. In spatialCorrelationGeneExp() this column holds \((b_x + 1) / (B + 1)\) for a fixed number \(B\) of permutations, also unadjusted; its adjustment across genes is that function's pValuePermuteXAdj.

pValuePermuteY

The same for the direction that permutes y, \((b_y + 1) / (L + 1)\). Not adjusted.

pValuePermute

The permutation p-value of the gene, which combines the two directions: exceedances / L if the gene stopped early (stop = "exceedances"), otherwise \((\max(b_x, b_y) + 1) / (L + 1)\). This is the larger of the two directions' sequential p-values, which is valid without assuming that the two directions are independent (see Details); it equals max(pValuePermuteX, pValuePermuteY) for a gene that reached nPermutations (stop = "limit") and is slightly smaller, exceedances / L instead of (exceedances + 1) / (L + 1), for a gene that stopped early. Not adjusted; its smallest possible value is 1 / (nPermutations + 1). The legacy functions have no such column: they adjust each direction on its own (pValuePermuteXAdj, pValuePermuteYAdj).

pValuePermuteAdj

pValuePermute adjusted across the tested genes with adjustMethod (stats::p.adjust(); skipped and failed genes are not counted). This is the column to use to call a gene significant.

nPermutations

The number of permutations \(L\) the gene used in each direction: fewer than the nPermutations argument when the gene stopped early, equal to it otherwise. The sum of this column is the work of the call.

stop

Why the permutations stopped: "exceedances" (early: a direction reached exceedances null correlations at least as extreme as the observed one), "limit" (the nPermutations argument was reached without that, so pValuePermute is \((\max(b_x, b_y) + 1) / (L + 1)\)), "skipped" (not tested) or "failed".

deltaStarMedianX, deltaStarMedianY

The median over the permutations of delta star, the bandwidth of delta whose surrogate variogram matched best, when x and when y is permuted. The same quantities as in spatialCorrelationGeneExp().

deltaGridEdge

TRUE when, in either direction, more than half of the permutations chose the smallest or the largest delta of the grid used (attr(result, "params")$deltaGrid): the best bandwidth may lie outside the grid, so consider extending delta. NA with fewer than 3 deltas.

percentSimilarity

The proportion (between 0 and 1, despite the name) of the kept pixels with \(|\log_2(y / x)| \le\) foldChange: the gene's spatial similarity. The same as in spatialSimilarity().

percentDissimilarityX

The proportion of the kept pixels with \(\log_2(y / x) < -\)foldChange: higher in x. The same as in spatialSimilarity().

percentDissimilarityY

The proportion of the kept pixels with \(\log_2(y / x) >\) foldChange: higher in y. The same as in spatialSimilarity().

numPixelInThresh

The number of kept pixels: those whose value is above t1 in x or above t2 in y. The same as in spatialSimilarity().

t1, t2

The gene's expression thresholds in x and in y: its minQuantile quantile in each sample. The same as in spatialSimilarity().

status

"ok", "skipped" (not tested for correlation: constant or rarely detected in a sample) or "failed" (see Details).

message

Why a gene was skipped or failed, or why its similarity is NA (negative values); empty otherwise.

The result has four attributes:

params

A list of the settings used: every argument after its default was applied (tests, nPermutations, exceedances, delta, maxDistPrctile, minDetected, surrogate, foldChange, minQuantile, minPixels, adjustMethod, seed, nThreads, progress, verbose, keepNulls), plus samples (the two sample labels), assay (the assay used in each sample), nPixels (the number of shared pixels), genes, deltaGrid (the deltas actually used, after the unusable ones were dropped) and minDetectedPixels (the number of detected pixels a gene needed in each sample to be tested; NA without the correlation test).

call

The matched call.

runtime

The run time, as proc.time() measures it.

details

Only with keepNulls = TRUE: a list with one element per gene, each a list of the null correlations (nullX, nullY) and the delta stars (deltaStarX, deltaStarY) of its permutations, in permutation order, when x and when y is permuted (empty for genes that were not tested).

print(), summary() and as.data.frame() (which returns a plain data frame) have methods for it (STcompareResult); a selection of rows keeps the class and the attributes, and a selection of columns is a plain data frame.

Details

Input. The two samples must share their pixels: rasterize them together, in one call such as SEraster::rasterizeGeneExpression(list(x, y), ...), so that a pixel name means the same location in both. The pixels used are those whose names (column names) are in both objects, in the column order of x, and their coordinates (SpatialExperiment::spatialCoords()) must agree.

Spatial correlation test. The observed statistic is Pearson's correlation r of the gene's values in x and y over the shared pixels. Its null distribution comes from spatially autocorrelated permutations (Viladomat et al. 2014): the values of x are shuffled across the pixels, smoothed with a Gaussian kernel whose window holds a share \(\delta\) of the pixels, and rescaled with added noise so that their variogram matches the variogram of x; the \(\delta\) of delta whose variogram matches best (delta star) is kept, the values of this surrogate are replaced by the gene's own values in the surrogate's rank order (surrogate = "remap", the default; see Rank-remapped surrogates), and its correlation with y is one null correlation. The same is done with y permuted and correlated with x. If there are more than 1000 shared pixels, the variograms use a random subsample of 1000 of them, drawn from seed with R's default random number generator whatever RNGkind() is set to. The smoother and the variogram are those of the other correlation functions of the package (spatialCorrelationGeneExp()).

Adaptive p-values. The permutations of a gene stop as soon as its p-value is clearly not small (Besag and Clifford 1991). Both directions (x permuted, y permuted) run in lockstep, and a gene stops at the first permutation \(L\) at which either direction has exceedances null correlations whose absolute value is at least \(|r|\), or at nPermutations. Its p-value (pValuePermute) is exceedances / L if it stopped early, and otherwise \((\max(b_x, b_y) + 1) / (L + 1)\), where \(b_x\) and \(b_y\) count the exceedances of each direction. This is the larger of the two directions' sequential p-values, each \(h / L\) when the direction stopped the gene (\(b = h\)) and \((b + 1) / (L + 1)\) at the limit, so it needs no assumption about how the two directions are related: if the observed correlation is distributed like the null correlations of either direction, \(P(p \le \alpha) \le \alpha\) at every \(\alpha\). The surrogates approximate that null distribution; with surrogate = "gaussian" the approximation fails for genes detected in few pixels (see Rarely detected genes). A gene that is clearly not significant stops after a few dozen permutations, and a significant gene runs to nPermutations, which sets the smallest possible p-value, 1 / (nPermutations + 1). With exceedances = Inf every gene gets exactly nPermutations permutations. The columns pValuePermuteX and pValuePermuteY always hold \((b + 1) / (L + 1)\), so pValuePermute equals their maximum for a gene that reached nPermutations and is slightly smaller, \(h / L\) instead of \((h + 1) / (L + 1)\), for a gene that stopped early. pValuePermute is adjusted across the tested genes with adjustMethod, which gives pValuePermuteAdj.

Which p-value should I report? pValuePermuteAdj: the permutation p-value of the gene, adjusted for the number of genes tested. A gene with pValuePermuteAdj < 0.05 has spatial expression patterns that are correlated between the samples beyond what the spatial autocorrelation of each pattern explains, at a false discovery rate of 5 percent (with the default adjustMethod = "BH"). The unadjusted pValuePermute is the per-gene p-value to report next to it, and its smallest possible value is 1 / (nPermutations + 1). pValuePermuteX and pValuePermuteY are descriptive: they are not adjusted, and when a gene stops early the direction that did not reach exceedances has an inflated value. pValueNaive ignores the spatial autocorrelation and is far too small; it is reported only to show how much the permutation test matters. The legacy spatialCorrelationGeneExp() returns the same unadjusted pValuePermuteX and pValuePermuteY (for a fixed number of permutations), plus each of them adjusted across genes, pValuePermuteXAdj and pValuePermuteYAdj; all four are per direction, and there is no combined p-value: the published analyses called a gene significant when both adjusted p-values were below 0.05.

Rank-remapped surrogates. With surrogate = "remap" (the default), the values of each surrogate are replaced by the gene's own values, placed in the rank order of the surrogate (the amplitude adjustment of the AAFT surrogates of Theiler et al. 1992, in a single step): the surrogate keeps the spatial arrangement of the smoothed, rescaled permutation and has exactly the distribution of values of the gene, zeros included. Delta star is chosen before the remapping, and for a gene with a spatial pattern the remapping is a monotone distortion of the surrogate's amplitudes, which changes its variogram a little. For a gene without spatial structure the ranks of its surrogates are close to uniformly random permutations, so its remapped surrogates are plain random permutations of its values and the test is the exact permutation test, whatever the gene's distribution (exactly so when the other gene has no spatial structure either). Many rearrangements of a gene detected in few pixels give exactly the observed correlation; as in the exact test, such ties count as exceedances (a null correlation within a relative 1e-9 of \(|r|\) counts, because cor() rounds each rearrangement differently). In simulations on the kidney and brain grids (bench/calibration-results.md in the source repository), remapped surrogates kept \(P(p \le \alpha) \le \alpha\) for independent genes detected in 1 to 100 percent of the pixels, had the same power as gaussian surrogates on correlated Gaussian fields, recovered the published kidney and brain genes at least as well, and cost about 7 percent more per permutation. surrogate = "gaussian" uses the surrogates as the smoothing and the added noise leave them. They are the surrogates of the other correlation functions of the package and of the published analyses, and are kept for comparability with them: their values are close to normally distributed, which gives p-values that are far too small for genes detected in few pixels (next paragraph) and conservative ones for skewed genes with a spatial pattern.

Rarely detected genes. Gaussian surrogates are smoothed and mixed with Gaussian noise, so their values are close to normally distributed. A gene detected in few pixels has a few high values among many zeros, and the correlation of two such genes is dominated by the few pixels where both are detected: chance coincidences give extreme correlations more often than gaussian surrogates do, so small p-values are too small, ten times or more for genes detected in one or two pixels. With surrogate = "gaussian", genes detected in fewer than a share minDetected of the shared pixels of either sample are therefore not tested for correlation (status = "skipped"). A gene is detected at a pixel where its value is above its lowest value over the shared pixels (for counts and normalized counts: where it is not zero). With gaussian surrogates the default asks for \(\sqrt{N}\) of the \(N\) shared pixels (18 of 311, 47 of 2170): the departure from the surrogates grows roughly as \(N / (k_x k_y)\) for genes detected in \(k_x\) and \(k_y\) pixels, and this removes the genes for which it is largest; sparse or zero-inflated genes above it can still get p-values that are somewhat too small, so with gaussian surrogates test the genes with a spatial pattern in both samples, or raise minDetected. Remapped surrogates have the gene's own values, and the problem disappears: in the simulations their p-values were calibrated down to genes detected in a single pixel, so with surrogate = "remap" the default minDetected is 0 and every gene that is not constant in a sample is tested. Such genes cost little (a gene without spatial structure stops after about ten permutations), and a gene detected in a single pixel cannot get a p-value below \(1 / N\): the exact test is discrete.

Spatial similarity. The same computation as spatialSimilarity(): for each gene, pixels are kept when their value is above the gene's minQuantile quantile in x or in y; zeros among them are replaced by 1e-4; percentSimilarity is the proportion of kept pixels with \(|\log_2(y / x)| \le\) foldChange. It is NA when fewer than a share minPixels of the pixels are kept. A fold change needs values that are not negative (counts or normalized expression on a linear scale): for a gene with negative values the similarity is NA, and a warning lists such genes.

Reproducibility. The permutations and the noise of each gene and direction come from their own random stream, which depends only on seed, the gene's name, the direction and the permutation number. The results therefore do not depend on nThreads, on the order of the genes, or on which other genes are in the call (except pValuePermuteAdj, which is adjusted over the tested genes), and the global random number generator (.Random.seed) is left unchanged. The permutations are drawn over the shared pixels in the column order of x (the order of y does not matter), and each direction has its own streams: reordering the pixels of x, or swapping x and y, gives other permutations and p-values that differ within Monte Carlo error. Results are deterministic on a given platform; the normal deviates use the C library's log() and can differ in the last bits between platforms.

Run time. It is proportional to the total number of permutations (the sum of the nPermutations column), and the work of all genes is shared by nThreads threads. With the defaults, genes that are clearly not significant use a few dozen permutations each and significant genes 10000, so the run time is dominated by the significant genes. A smaller nPermutations, such as 1000, was 6 to 7 times faster on the published data and still resolves p-values down to 1 / 1001.

Skipped and failed genes. A gene that is constant in a sample (for example never detected) or detected in fewer pixels than minDetected asks for (by default only with surrogate = "gaussian") is not tested for correlation: it gets status = "skipped", NA p-values and the reason in message (its similarity is still computed), and one message counts such genes. A gene that cannot be tested gets status = "failed", NA in the statistics that could not be computed, and the reason in message; one warning lists the failed genes, and the other genes are not affected. This happens for genes with missing or infinite values on the shared pixels (every statistic is NA) and when the permutations of a gene fail (for example a degenerate variogram fit).

References

Viladomat J, Mazumder R, McInturff A, McCauley DJ, Hastie T (2014). Assessing the significance of global and local correlations under spatial autocorrelation: a nonparametric approach. Biometrics 70(2):409-418. doi:10.1111/biom.12139

Besag J, Clifford P (1991). Sequential Monte Carlo p-values. Biometrika 78(2):301-304. doi:10.1093/biomet/78.2.301

Theiler J, Eubank S, Longtin A, Galdrikian B, Farmer JD (1992). Testing for nonlinearity in time series: the method of surrogate data. Physica D 58(1-4):77-94. doi:10.1016/0167-2789(92)90102-S

See also

spatialCorrelationGeneExp() and spatialSimilarity(), which reproduce the published analyses exactly. The tutorials: vignette("getting-started-with-STcompare", package = "STcompare"), vignette("how-STcompare-works", package = "STcompare") and vignette("parameters-performance-reproducibility", package = "STcompare").

Examples

data(speKidney)
# rasterize the three samples together, onto one grid of pixels
rast <- SEraster::rasterizeGeneExpression(speKidney, assay_name = "counts",
                                          resolution = 0.2, fun = "mean",
                                          square = FALSE)

# A and B have opposite spatial patterns, A and C similar ones
ab <- compareSpatial(list(A = rast$A, B = rast$B), nPermutations = 999,
                     nThreads = 2)
#> compareSpatial: 1 gene on 273 shared pixels in 0.2 s (999 permutations in total, 2 threads)
ab
#> STcompareResult: 1 gene on 273 shared pixels; A vs B (assay pixelval)
#> Correlation: adaptive permutation p-values (stop at 10 exceedances, at most 999 permutations); 11 deltas from 0.01 to 0.9; rank-remapped surrogates
#>   pValuePermuteAdj < 0.05: 1 gene (0 with correlationCoef > 0, 1 with correlationCoef < 0)
#>   stopped early: 0; reached nPermutations: 1; skipped: 0; failed: 0
#> Similarity (|log2(y / x)| <= 1): median percentSimilarity 0.535 (0 genes with NA)
#> 
#>  gene nPixels correlationCoef pValueNaive pValuePermuteX pValuePermuteY
#>  Gene     273          -0.947   5.65e-136          0.001          0.001
#>  pValuePermute pValuePermuteAdj nPermutations  stop deltaStarMedianX
#>          0.001            0.001           999 limit              0.2
#>  deltaStarMedianY deltaGridEdge percentSimilarity percentDissimilarityX
#>               0.2         FALSE             0.535                 0.267
#>  percentDissimilarityY numPixelInThresh   t1   t2 status message
#>                  0.198              273 9.87 7.67     ok        
ac <- compareSpatial(list(A = rast$A, C = rast$C), nPermutations = 999,
                     nThreads = 2)
#> compareSpatial: 1 gene on 277 shared pixels in 0.2 s (999 permutations in total, 2 threads)
summary(ac)
#> compareSpatial: 1 gene on 277 shared pixels (A vs C); 1 ok, 0 skipped, 0 failed
#> Correlation, pValuePermuteAdj < 0.05: 1 gene (1 with correlationCoef > 0, 0 with correlationCoef < 0)
#>   stopped early: 0; reached nPermutations: 1; skipped: 0; failed: 0
#>   nPermutations per gene: median 999, max 999; 999 in total
#>   settings: nPermutations = 999, exceedances = 10, 11 deltas (0.01 to 0.9), rank-remapped surrogates, BH adjustment, seed 0
#> Similarity, percentSimilarity:
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>       0       0       0       0       0       0 
#> Run time: 0.2 s
as.data.frame(ac)[, c("gene", "correlationCoef", "pValuePermute",
                      "pValuePermuteAdj", "nPermutations", "percentSimilarity")]
#>      gene correlationCoef pValuePermute pValuePermuteAdj nPermutations
#> Gene Gene       0.9431531         0.001            0.001           999
#>      percentSimilarity
#> Gene                 0
